title: Wound Care in Nonhuman Species: An Integrated Framework Applied to Central African Chimpanzees
content:
This novel methodological framework standardizes wounds and wound-tending behaviors across diverse animal taxa and demonstrates its application to the behavior of individuals of a group of Central African chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes troglodytes) living in the wild. By combining a cross-species standardized ethogram with a distance-based wound impact scoring system, the framework quantifies the dynamic relationship between behavior and healing, enabling systematic comparative research across species.


ABSTRACT

Wound care represents a major challenge across species, with impaired wound healing imposing substantial costs on health, survival, and fitness. Insights from nonhuman animals offer promising avenues for understanding wound-management strategies and identifying novel therapeutic compounds. Yet, despite the strong consequences of wound healing for survival and fitness—especially in free-living populations—wound-management strategies remain poorly understood. A key limitation is that existing methods for evaluating wound characteristics rely on close-range observations, leaving a substantial gap for species that cannot be observed up close. As a result, the diversity of wound-tending behaviors and their relationship to wound condition and healing remain little understood. We introduce a novel methodological framework and demonstrate its application to Central African chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes troglodytes) living in the wild. The framework merges two complementary components: (1) a systematic classification of wound-tending behaviors in nonhuman species by establishing a standardized ethogram; and (2) a structured, distance-based assessment of wound impact, based on multiple observable characteristics. By combining a systematic behavioral classification with a distance-based scoring system, the framework overcomes key limitations of existing approaches. The proposed method is flexible, feasible, and transferable across species, facilitating systematic comparative research on health-related behaviors.
